To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

magnetic transcranial stimulation (TMS) can be used to investigate excitatory and inhibiting mechanisms in acute strokes and that the association between shortening in the silent period (SP) with increasing voluntary contraction of the target muscle in acute strokes may be a good predictor of eventual recovery after 3 months.

the excitatory and inhibitive mechanisms of the brain are differently affected after stroke, and that the shortening of the inhibitive mechanism with increasing voluntary contraction of the target muscle is a predictor of poor recovery of the patient.

the excitability of the cortico-spinal pathway, measured by the amplitude of MEPs, was increased, while the inhibition, measured by the duration of the silent period (SP), was decreased, in acute stroke.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the dissociation of excitability changes in the motor cortex of patients with acute and chronic stroke.
the study of the excitatory/inhibitory mechanisms of the central motor pathways in acute and chronic stroke.
a better understanding of the mechanisms underlying the recovery process of stroke patients.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the excitatory and inhibiting pathways are differentially affected after a cerebral ischaemic stroke, and the excitatory mechanisms are more likely to be affected in the acute phase of the stroke.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the excitatory and inhibitive mechanisms are dissociated in acute stroke, and that the SPD pattern may be a useful clinical tool to predict the eventual recovery of the stroke.
in the acute stage of the stroke, the excitatory and inhibiting mechanisms are still preserved, whereas in the chronic stage of the stroke the inhibitory mechanisms are impaired.
the MEP-amplitues and SPD are sensitive to the excitatory and inhibatory mechanisms in acute strokes.
The main takeaway from our work is that
magnetic transcranial stimulation can be a powerful tool to study excitatory and inhibatory mechanisms in the motor system and their possible changes in acute and chronic stroke.
the combination of MEP-amplitudes with SPDs may be a useful clinical tool to evaluate the excitatory and inhibatory mechanisms in acute stroke and to predict eventual recovery of the stroke.

the combination of MEP-amplitudes with SPD patterns may help us to understand the pathophysiology of the motor system in the early stages of stroke and to predict the evolution of the motor deficit in the acute phase of cerebral ischaemia.
